An AI agent can now watch it paint a pixel-art sprite, step by step, in your browser. The project is called Claude pxl. It shows you exactly how the art is being drawn, like a timelapse of a painter at work. You can watch the AI add colors, shapes, and lights in real time.

Caption:
Training an AI to Drive with Natural Selection

A self-driving car does what you do, many times a second: look, decide, act. Looking turns the road into numbers (how far is that wall? how fast am I going?). Deciding is a function that turns those numbers into gas, brake and steering.

This car sees seven numbers: how far the walls are along five yellow lines, its speed, and its direction. Its function is a small neural network with 434 weights, and nobody set them. I made twenty random ones and let them race; most crashed at once. The ones that got furthest became parents, and their children are copies with small random changes. Generation 33 finished the first lap. By generation 4,000 they race through every corner, on lines they found themselves.

In the literature this is called neuroevolution: a neural network trained by selection and mutation alone, with no gradients.

#AI #neuralnetwork #evolution #selfdriving #machinelearning

Caption:
Google dropped a banger paper 🧠

If you write or curate skills for your agents, this one is for you.

Agent skills are folders holding the instructions an agent follows for a task. People increasingly let agents write those instructions themselves.

The loop is simple: run the agent on some tasks, read the runs that failed, rewrite the instructions, and keep the rewrite only if the score goes up on a held-out validation set.

Here is where it breaks.

Working out why the agent failed means reading full traces and comparing failed runs against successful ones. But that diagnosis never gets written down. The only thing saved is the new instruction text it produced.

So when that instruction reverts, the finding behind it goes too. The next round reads the same failures, reaches the same conclusion, and often proposes the fix that already lost, with no memory that it was ever tried.

WikiSkill fixes this by splitting the one folder into three:

1️⃣ Raw traces, written once and never touched

2️⃣ A wiki of accumulated knowledge holding what keeps breaking, what has worked, and every edit tried so far with the reason it passed or failed. Nothing here is ever deleted.

3️⃣ The skills themselves, reverted whenever an edit makes things worse

The instructions can roll back, but the understanding behind them never does.

An early skill gets rejected for being too vague. Instead of vanishing, that rejection is logged. The next round sees the vague version failed and writes a concrete rule instead. Same failure, same analysis, but the second attempt starts from knowing what already did not work.

Turning the knowledge layer off drops the average score by about a quarter.

Two other results worth noting: smaller models with evolved skills beat much larger models running without any, and skills evolved by one model transfer across families.

WikiSkill: Compiling Agent Experience into Persistent Knowledge for Skill Evolution

Liyan Tang¹, Cyrus Rashtchian¹, Chun-Sung Ferng¹, Andrew Tomkins¹, Da-Cheng Juan¹ and Tu Vu¹,²
¹Google Research, ²Virginia Tech

Agent skills package specialized knowledge and workflows into reusable resources that extend AI agent capabilities. Recent work automatically discovers such skills from agent experience, which enables agents to progressively adapt through interaction. However, the insights that guide skill development typically remain scattered across optimization histories, limiting their systematic reuse across iterations. We introduce WikiSkill, a framework that co-evolves agent skills with a persistent knowledge base (wiki). At a high level, WikiSkill separates raw execution experience, accumulated knowledge, and executable skills, while continuously consolidating experience into the wiki, which subsequent skill updates can build on. Across diverse benchmarks and models, WikiSkill consistently outperforms state-of-the-art skill-evolution methods and improves over no-skill baselines in most model-benchmark settings. We find that skill evolution complements model scaling: larger models generally benefit more from evolved skills, while smaller models with skills can outperform substantially larger models without them. We also find that evolved skills transfer effectively across models and model families, and skills evolved by other models can outperform self-evolved skills. Finally, our ablation studies confirm that persistent knowledge accumulation in the wiki is critical for effective skill evolution. These results demonstrate the benefits of systematically accumulating and refining agent experience for developing reusable and transferable skills.

Caption:
Evolution of agent landscape from 2022-26 🔄

The biggest shift in AI agents had nothing to do with making models smarter. It was about making the environment around them smarter.

Here's how agent engineering evolved in just 4 years, across three distinct phases:

Phase 1: Weights (2022)
Everything was about the model itself. Bigger models, more data, better training. RLHF and fine-tuning shaped behavior. If you wanted a better agent, you trained a better model.

This worked great for single-turn tasks but hit a wall fast. Updating one fact meant retraining. Auditing behavior was nearly impossible.

Phase 2: Context (2023-2024)
The realization: you don't always need to change the model. You can change what the model sees.

Prompt engineering, few-shot examples, chain-of-thought, RAG. Suddenly the same frozen model could behave completely differently based on what you put in front of it.

But context windows are finite. Long prompts get noisy. Models attend unevenly. Every session starts fresh with zero memory.

Context made agents flexible. It didn't make them reliable.

Phase 3: Harness Engineering (2025-2026)
This is where we are now, and the shift is fundamental.

The question changed from "what should we tell the model?" to "what environment should the model operate in?"

The model sits inside a harness that includes persistent memory, reusable skills, standardized protocols like MCP, execution sandboxes, approval gates, and observability layers.

Same model. Completely different reliability.

A coding agent implementing a feature: without a harness, the model keeps everything in a fragile prompt. With a harness, persistent memory supplies context, skill files encode conventions, and the runtime handles failures.

1. What You're Building
A shopkeeper types KC-4471 into a help centre. Vector search returns three articles about other error codes: an expired login, a wrong UPI ID and a pending payment. The article for KC-4471 doesn't even make its top 10.
This isn't a broken embedding model. Embeddings capture meaning, and to a meaning model KC-4471, KC-4714 and KC-6016 are nearly the same thing: "some error code". Exact IDs, version numbers, part numbers and rare names are where vector search quietly fails. Real knowledge bases are full of them.
You'll fix it with the three-stage setup used in production search:

Stage | Tool | Job
Keyword search | BM25 (rank_bm25) | Finds articles that contain the exact token, like 4471
Vector search | MiniLM vectors in Chroma | Finds articles that mean the same thing in different words

Build Hybrid Search That Actually Beats Vector Search - in 45 Minutes   2

Slide 4:
Stage | Tool | Job
Fusion | Reciprocal Rank Fusion | Merges both lists by rank, so neither score scale dominates
Reranking | bge-reranker-base cross-encoder | Reads question and article together and puts the best one first

Everything runs on your laptop. There's no LLM and no API key, because retrieval is the whole point here. Whatever your RAG app answers is limited by what this step hands it.
Every tool here is free so you can follow along without a credit card. That makes it a good stack to learn on, not necessarily the best one to ship. Where a paid or managed option does a step better, the section on that step says so.
On 20 labelled questions, vector search puts the right article first 12 times. Hybrid search with reranking does it 16 times. On the 12 questions that hinge on a code or a name, the score goes from 6 to 10. You'll also see where each part fails, including the reranker.

2. Architecture Overview
Question → BM25 keyword search → Reciprocal Rank Fusion → Top 10 candidates → Cross-encoder reranker → Ranked results
Question → Vector search in Chroma → Reciprocal Rank Fusion

The question goes to two retrievers at once. BM25 scores every article by the exact words it shares with the question, giving extra weight to rare words. Vector search embeds the question with MiniLM and asks Chroma for the 10 nearest article vectors.
Reciprocal Rank Fusion merges the two top-10 lists. It ignores the raw scores completely and looks only at each article's position in each list. That matters, because a BM25 score of 6.5 and a cosine similarity of 0.445 aren't on the same scale.

Build Hybrid Search That Actually Beats Vector Search - in 45 Minutes   3

Slide 5:
The merged top 10 go to the reranker. It's a cross-encoder, which means it reads the question and one article together as a single input and outputs one relevance score. That's slower than comparing two vectors, but it's far more accurate. You only run it on 10 candidates, never the whole corpus.
The demo prints five methods side by side, so you can see what each stage adds: vector, bm25, hybrid (RRF only), vector+rerank and hybrid+rerank.

What lives where
When you run the program, you start one Python process on your laptop. Every piece below sits in that process's memory, and there's no database server or search server involved. Some pieces are built once at startup. Others do their work fresh for every question.

Piece | Built once at startup | Done for every question | Where it lives
Article text | The DOCS dictionary: id to text | Looked up by id | Python memory
BM25 index | Word counts per article, how rare each word is, each article's length | Scores all 55 articles against the question's words, returns the top 10 ids | Python memory, in the BM25Index object
Vector index | One 384-number vector per article, added to Chroma | Embeds the question, asks Chroma for the 10 nearest vectors | Chroma, running in memory inside the same process
Fusion (RRF) | Nothing, it's a function | Takes the two lists of ids and returns one merged list | Nothing stored
Top 10 candidates | Nothing | The first 10 ids of the merged list, as a plain Python list | A variable that's gone after the question
Reranker | The model's weights (about 1.1 GB) | Scores 10 question-and-article pairs, returns them sorted | Model in memory, no index at all

Build Hybrid Search That Actually Beats Vector Search - in 45 Minutes   4

Slide 6:
Two things to notice. First, nothing is stored between questions: a search result is just a list of ids that gets used and dropped. Second, nothing is stored between runs either. Both indexes are rebuilt from DOCS every time you start the program, which takes a moment for 55 articles.
A real app would keep a server running that builds the indexes once and answers many requests from them. For large collections, the indexes would be saved to disk. That's the main thing a search engine like Elasticsearch or Qdrant does for you.

How each piece works, on one question
The table says where things live. Here's what each piece does, following the question KC-4471 through the pipeline. The sections after this build each one in code.
BM25 reads the question as words. It splits KC-4471 into kc-4471, kc and 4471, then scores each article by how many of those words it contains. A word that's in only a few articles counts for more. 4471 is in one article and kc is in all 21 error articles, so the 4471 article scores 6.5, the next best scores 0.5, and most articles score 0.
Vector search reads the question as meaning. MiniLM turns the question into 384 numbers, and Chroma returns the 10 articles whose numbers are closest. The model was trained to place similar meanings near each other, not to match exact characters. To it, KC-4471 looks like "some error code", so it returns other error articles. Its best match is the login error KC-6016.
RRF merges the two lists using positions. It takes the 10 ids from BM25 and the 10 from vector search. Each article earns 1 / (60 + position) from every list it appears in, and the earnings are added up. The right article is first in BM25 but missing from vector search's list, so it earns only one share and lands 7th. Articles that both lists like outrank it.
The top 10 candidates are the first 10 ids of the merged list. That's all they are: a short Python list. The cut exists because of the next step. The reranker has to read every candidate in full, so its time grows with the list. Scoring 10 took about 250 ms in our runs and scoring 20 took about 530 ms. The cut also has to be wide enough to contain the right article, which is why fusion matters: it got KC-4471 into the 10.

Slide 7:
The reranker reads the question and each candidate together. It's given a pair, KC-4471 and one article's text, and outputs a relevance score. Because both texts are in the same input, it can see that 4471 appears in the question and in the article, and that 4714 doesn't match. It scores all 10 pairs, and KC-4471 gets 0.975. The near-twin KC-4481 gets 0.931, and every other candidate is close to zero. That puts KC-4471 first, but only just.

1. What You're Building
A new billing clerk joins a Bengaluru distributor. Nobody hands them a manual. They price an invoice, the accountant sends back a correction, and they write the lesson in a notebook. A month later the notebook is the manual.
You'll build that clerk as an agent. It prices GST invoices for a made-up company, Kaveri Traders, which has four billing rules nobody writes down. The agent is never told them. After each wrong answer it reads the accountant's correction and adds one bullet to its own playbook, a JSON file on disk.
On eight invoices it has never seen, the empty playbook gets 4 of 16 attempts right (only the two easy controls). After one pass over ten training invoices, the agent's three-bullet playbook gets 16 of 16. No fine-tuning, no weights changed. Only the text in front of the model changed.
The method is ACE, Agentic Context Engineering (Zhang et al., Stanford, SambaNova and UC Berkeley, ICLR 2026). It splits the work across three roles:
Role | Job
Generator | Does the task, using the playbook, and says which bullets it used

Slide 4:
Role | Job
Reflector | Compares the answer with the ground truth and finds the lesson
Curator | Turns the lesson into a small delta: a few new bullets, never a rewrite
The delta is the idea worth learning. Most "self-improving prompt" setups ask an LLM to rewrite the whole prompt after each mistake. ACE treats the playbook like a git repo instead: you add a line, and nothing else moves. In the paper, ACE beat strong baselines by 10.6% on agent tasks and 8.6% on finance tasks.
2. Architecture Overview
Invoice → Generator → Checker: exact total? / Accountant correction → Reflector → Curator: ADD bullets / Votes: helpful or harmful → Python merge and prune → Playbook JSON
The Generator reads the whole playbook and the invoice, and returns a total plus the IDs of the bullets it relied on. A plain Python checker compares that total with the true one.
If the answer is wrong, the Reflector sees the clerk's working and the accountant's line-by-line correction. It names the missed rule and votes on each bullet the clerk used: helpful, harmful or neutral.
The Curator reads that lesson and returns only the new bullets to ADD. Then plain Python does the rest. It gives each bullet an ID, skips near-duplicates, bumps the vote counters, and drops any bullet that has misled the clerk more often than it helped.
That last part matters most. The purple boxes are LLM calls. The green merge box is ordinary code. No LLM ever writes the playbook file. The official ACE code works the same way, and its Curator can only ADD.

Most demos in this series forget everything when the program exits. This one doesn't. The playbook is a file, so a second run of train starts with everything the first run learned. That is the whole point: the agent gets better across runs, and the model never changes.
How each piece works, on one invoice
Training invoice T01 is 12 bags of basmati rice at Rs 455 with 5% GST, plus Rs 650 freight. With an empty playbook, the Generator taxes the freight at 5% like the rice and answers Rs 6,383. The truth is Rs 6,500, because Kaveri Traders always taxes freight at 18%.
The Reflector reads the correction, which has a line saying "GST on freight, always @18%". It returns the insight "Freight charges attract 18% GST... product GST rates apply only to product line items."
The Curator turns that into one ADD operation. Python stores it as [rul-00001] Apply 18% GST to all freight (non-product) charges regardless of the product GST rates. On T04, three invoices later, the Generator uses rul-00001, gets the answer right, and the Reflector votes it helpful. Its counter goes to helpful=1.

5. The Invoices and the Hidden Rules
The agent needs work where it will fail at first, for reasons it can't guess. Kaveri Traders has four billing rules:
1. Freight is always taxed at 18%, whatever rate the goods carry.
2. The trade discount applies to goods only, never to freight.
3. GST is rounded to the nearest rupee on every line, then summed.

1. What You're Building
A RAG bot gives you an answer and hides how it got there. When the answer is wrong, you can't see whether retrieval missed the right passage, served a misleading one, or never had the answer at all.
You'll build a debugger that opens that box. It runs an ordinary Chroma retriever. Then an LLM judge reads a wider pool of passages next to it and marks which ones actually answer the question. Every step is timed and saved as a trace.
The payoff is a verdict per question: HEALTHY, NOISY_CONTEXT, RETRIEVAL_MISS or CORPUS_GAP. Each one points at a different fix.

2. Architecture Overview
Question → Chroma retriever top 10 → Cut to top-k 3 → Answer model → Trace JSON → Rich terminal view
Chroma retriever top 10 → LLM judge reads all 10 → Diagnose → Trace JSON

The top row is the pipeline under test: retrieve, keep the top 3, answer. That's the black box. Only those 3 passages ever reach the answer model.
The judge sits beside it. It reads all 10 passages the retriever found and labels each one. It never removes or adds anything, so the trace shows the pipeline exactly as it runs.
Put the two views together and every passage lands in one of four cells:

|reached the prompt | HIT | NOISE |
|cut by retrieval | MISS | CUT |

A MISS is the interesting one. The answer existed, the retriever even found it, and the top-k cut threw it away. No amount of prompt tuning fixes that.

8. The Judge - a Second Opinion on Every Passage
LLM-as-judge means using a model to grade another system's output. Here, the judge grades the retriever. It reads each passage and says whether it answers the question.
A judge that can see the retriever's ranking tends to agree with it, and a judge that agrees with the retriever can't debug it. So this one never sees similarity scores or ranks, and the passages arrive shuffled.
It also returns a label, not a number. Ask a model for a 0-1 confidence and you tend to get 0.95 on everything. Three named labels force a real decision:
• answers: the passage, read alone, gives a correct and direct answer
• partial: same topic, but it misses the part the question asks about
• unrelated: a different topic

def client() -> AsyncGroq:
    """One shared async Groq client."""
    global _client
    if _client is None:
        _client = AsyncGroq(api_key=config.require_api_key())

def shuffled_labels(candidates: list[Candidate]) -> dict[str, Candidate]:
    """Give each passage a neutral label (c1, c2...) in an order unrelated to its rank."""
    ordered = sorted(candidates, key=lambda c: hashlib.sha256(c.pid.encode()).hexdigest())
    return {f"c{i}": c for i, c in enumerate(ordered, start=1)}

        "type": "object",
        "additionalProperties": False,
        "required": ["verdicts"],
        "properties": {

async def _call_judge(messages: list[dict], schema: dict) -> tuple[dict, int]:
    """Send one strict-schema request, retrying once if gpt-oss breaks the schema."""
    for attempt in range(2):
        try:
            response = await client().chat.completions.create(
                model=config.JUDGE_MODEL,
                messages=messages,
                temperature=0.0,
                reasoning_effort="low",
                max_completion_tokens=config.JUDGE_MAX_TOKENS,
                response_format={
                    "type": "json_schema",
                    "json_schema": {"name": "verdicts", "strict": True, "schema": schema},
                },
            )
        except BadRequestError as exc:
            if "json_validate_failed" in str(exc) and attempt == 0:
                continue
            raise
        return json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content), response.usage.total_tokens
    raise RuntimeError("unreachable")

1. What You're Building
Plain RAG searches its knowledge base on every question. Ask it to convert 5 km to miles and it still runs a vector search, stuffs two unrelated passages into the prompt, and then says "I don't know". Ask it something vague like "What's the limit?" and it grabs the closest passage and answers confidently about the wrong limit.
This agent thinks before it searches. It reads the question and makes one of three calls:

Decision | When | What happens
retrieve | The answer depends on company-specific facts | Search the handbook, grade what came back, answer, check the answer
direct | General knowledge any model already has | Answer straight away, no search
clarify | Too vague to answer | Ask the user what they meant

The idea comes from Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2023). The model emits reflection tokens that steer its own pipeline: [Retrieve] decides whether to search, [IsRel] grades each passage, [IsSup] checks the answer is backed by the passages, and [IsUse] checks it actually helps.
If you built the self-healing RAG agent from the earlier post, this is its next step. That one retrieved every time and graded only the final answer. This one adds the gate in front, and grades passages and answers separately.
You'll build it as an internal help bot for a made-up startup, Dabba Labs. On nine test questions, plain RAG gets 3 right and the self-RAG agent gets 9. The agent also spends more tokens, and Section 13 shows exactly why.

Every question hits the gate first, a single Gemini call that returns retrieve, direct or clarify as JSON. direct and clarify each take one more call and finish. They never touch the vector store.
On the retrieve path, Chroma returns the 2 closest handbook passages. The IsRel call labels each one relevant or irrelevant. If nothing is relevant, the agent rewrites the question into handbook vocabulary and searches once more.
The relevant passages go to the generator. The IsSup / IsUse call then checks the draft. A failing draft gets one stricter redraft, and if that still fails, the answer goes out with a visible caveat instead of being hidden.
The Self-RAG paper fine-tunes a model to produce these tokens. Here a normal model produces them as JSON with a fixed set of allowed values, so you get the same decision points without training anything.

def _retry_delay(err: errors.APIError) -> float:
    """Seconds Gemini asks us to wait (its RetryInfo, e.g. '9.5s'), or 15 if it doesn't say."""
    for item in (err.details or {}).get("error", {}).get("details", []):
        if item.get("@type", "").endswith("RetryInfo"):
            return float(item.get("retryDelay", "15s").rstrip("s"))
    return 15.0


async def _generate(prompt: str, config: types.GenerateContentConfig) -> types.GenerateContentResponse:
    """Send one request, waiting and retrying when Gemini says 429 (rate) or 503 (busy).

    A 429 that asks for a wait of minutes or hours is the DAILY quota, and no retry
    will help today, so it is raised at once. On a paid key, 429s are rare and 503s
    much rarer, so this loop almost never runs, but it costs nothing to keep.
    """
    for attempt in range(4):
        await _pace()
        try:
            return await client().aio.models.generate_content(
                model=MODEL, contents=prompt, config=config
            )
        except errors.APIError as err:
            if err.code not in (429, 503) or attempt == 3:
                raise
            delay = _retry_delay(err)
            if delay > 120:
                raise
            print(f"  (Gemini {err.code}, waiting {delay:.0f}s and retrying)")
            await asyncio.sleep(delay + 1)

def _config(schema: dict | None = None) -> types.GenerateContentConfig:
    """Build the call settings: temperature 0, minimal thinking, optional JSON schema."""

        temperature=0,

def _tokens(response: types.GenerateContentResponse) -> tuple[int, int]:
    """Return (input, output) tokens. Thinking tokens bill as output, so they count there."""
    usage = response.usage_metadata
    out = (usage.candidates_token_count or 0) + (usage.thoughts_token_count or 0)
    return usage.prompt_token_count or 0, out


async def ask_text(prompt: str) -> Reply:
    """Ask for a free-text reply."""
    response = await _generate(prompt, _config())
    return Reply((response.text or "").strip(), *_tokens(response))


async def ask_json(prompt: str, schema: dict) -> Reply:
    """Ask for a reply that must match the schema, and parse it into a dict."""
    response = await _generate(prompt, _config(schema))
    return Reply(json.loads(response.text), *_tokens(response))

The next step after Karpathy's autoresearch idea 🧠

Tuning an agent is mostly manual work: editing prompts, tools, and control flow by hand, then rerunning evals to see what moved.

Researchers have been building automated optimizers to do that outer loop instead. The underlying process is the same: an LLM proposes a change, an evaluator scores it, and the proposer reads that result before proposing the next one.

They differ in what they edit and what feedback they get to read.

1️⃣ GEPA (Berkeley) - Optimizes the text of a system like prompts, tool descriptions, or the agent's own code. Instead of collapsing a run into one scalar reward the way RL does, it reads the full execution trace, diagnoses why the run failed, and proposes a targeted fix. Converges in hundreds of rollouts instead of the thousands GRPO needs.

2️⃣ AutoResearch (inspired by Karpathy) - Runs a narrower version of the loop where a coding agent iterates on a program.md file, scores outputs against fixed evals, and keeps whatever improves.

3️⃣ Meta-Harness - Points the loop at the harness itself, the scaffolding code that decides what to retrieve, how to format it, and what state to keep between calls.

The natural question is which one to use. The answer is none of them alone.

On the Frontier-CS benchmark, holding model, thinking effort, and budget fixed, no optimizer wins everywhere. Across 10 tasks, GEPA led on 3, AutoResearch on 3, and Meta-Harness on 4.

Each optimizer hill-climbs fast and then stalls. But handing the stalled candidate to a different optimizer breaks the plateau since each one attacks the problem differently.

omni (open-source) already automates all of that. It runs every optimizer on a fraction of the budget, takes the best candidate, and hands it to a fresh optimizer to keep going. It scores 7.8 percentage points above the best standalone optimizer at the same budget.

GEPA (Genetic-Pareto) is a framework for optimizing any system with textual parameters against any evaluation metric. Unlike RL or gradient-based methods that collapse execution traces into a single scalar reward, GEPA uses LLMs to read full execution traces — error messages, profiling data, reasoning logs — to diagnose why a candidate failed and propose targeted fixes. Through iterative reflection, mutation, and Pareto-aware selection, GEPA evolves high-performing variants with minimal evaluations.
